title: Case notion discovery and recommendation: automated event log building on databases
research_question: Can candidate case notions for process mining be automatically discovered from complex databases and ranked by predicted event-log interestingness before the expensive event logs themselves are constructed?
methodology: The authors formalize database-oriented case notions using the OpenSLEX meta-model and define procedures for deriving case identifiers and event logs from connected database structures. They define structural event-log quality or interestingness measures and inexpensive predictors based on case-notion and dataset characteristics, implementing the workflow in the open-source eddytools package. Evaluation uses an SAP sample dataset containing 87 tables and generates 10,622 candidate case notions; actual generated logs provide ground-truth metric values. Prediction accuracy and recommendation quality are compared with regression and learning-to-rank methods, including fivefold cross-validation and NDCG@10.

key_findings.finding: The framework can systematically generate alternative database case notions and construct corresponding event logs, allowing multiple process perspectives to be explored from the same underlying data.
The authors' unsupervised predictors were substantially less accurate for individual log-property values than stronger supervised regressors such as quantile regression and neural-network regression.

Despite weak absolute prediction accuracy, the custom unsupervised predictor preserved relative interestingness well enough to provide useful rankings and outperformed the evaluated regressors on average for ranking quality.
Among the compared supervised ranking approaches, MART and Random Forest were the only algorithms whose median NDCG@10 exceeded the custom predictor's median in the reported comparison.

When labeled training data are available, supervised regressors are preferable for accurate property prediction and learning-to-rank methods such as Random Forest and MART provide stronger rankings; the proposed predictor is intended for settings without such training data.

The SAP evaluation generated 10,622 case-notion candidates from 87 tables, illustrating the combinatorial search problem that motivates predicting promising views before materializing every event log.

limitations: The proposed definition of log interestingness uses only structural properties such as support, level of detail, and average events per trace.
The interestingness metric ignores business semantics, activity meaningfulness, and behavioral homogeneity.
The relationship between the objective interestingness score and subjective judgments from business analysts or domain experts was not evaluated.
Individual predictions of event-log properties lack accuracy even when the resulting relative ranking is useful.
The approach assumes that the database schema and the locations or representation of events are already known, so event-data discovery itself still requires domain knowledge.
The main quantitative evaluation uses a single SAP sample dataset, limiting evidence for generalization across substantially different database environments.
raw_claims: Different ways of correlating database objects and events produce different process-mining case notions.
The framework represents these correlations formally so candidate event logs can be generated automatically.
The authors evaluate candidate logs using structural characteristics intended to represent interestingness.
Predicted interestingness can be calculated without first building every candidate event log.
The evaluation produces 10,622 candidate case notions from an SAP dataset containing 87 tables.
The custom unsupervised predictors are weak at estimating exact event-log property values.
Relative ranking quality is considerably better than the absolute prediction accuracy would suggest.
MART and Random Forest provide stronger rankings when suitable training data are available.
The unsupervised custom predictor remains useful because it requires no labeled training set.
The eddytools package implements the data preparation, case-notion discovery, and event-log building workflow.
The paper explicitly treats its structural definition of interestingness as incomplete and in need of user-centered validation.
